Can people truly change? 

 
Throughout education people are encouraged to challenge their views, be this on politics, history, philosophy or even more fundamental things about who they are. However, many of us find that there is a core set of beliefs that we struggle to abandon despite persistent and convincing arguments to the contrary. Consider for example how people’s beliefs on abortion are normally highly entrenched from a young age with very few people every changing their minds. Despite this, we still enter debates and conversations with them aiming to change their minds. 

We also have many other ways in which people might be believed to change. Prisoners after rehabilitation may reform from their crime ridden ways, people convert to religions late in their life and some give up drugs and alcohol despite deep addictions. But is this real change or merely reverting to some deeper core beliefs that were always present? Maybe instead the criminal was always good at heart, the religious convert always curious about a higher power and the reformed addict never truly an addict at heart. 

Furthermore, if we can change everything then what is it that makes us us? With no permanence how do we then move further to define ourselves. Can people ever truly change or is there some core inner self that is immoveable? Are there some beliefs, characteristics and traits that we can truly never change or is everything about us able to adapt to different arguments, beliefs, circumstances and environments? And if so, who are we? 

Credit to James for the thesis of the debate we'll be holding at 7:30 on Wednesday 14th of October in ER145. Come along for a chill debate and a trip to one of Durham's many lovely bars after!

We are proud to announce that our two-stage solid rocket, Rosemary IV, launched to altitude of 23.9km at the Friends of Amateur Rocketry (FAR) site in California — the highest a UK amateur rocket has flown! 

After achieving successful stage separation, Rosemary IV reached a top speed of Mach 2.85 (3519 km/h).

The launch of Rosemary IV marks the culmination of over a year of work, modifying our record-holding Rosemary III rocket to function as a sustainer in a two-stage configuration, and designing and manufacturing a booster. This made Rosemary IV the society's most high-powered rocket to date. The launch itself was a society-wide effort, drawing talent and expertise from across multiple projects this year and providing critical launch experience for many members. We are very grateful to our sponsors who made this project possible: Department of Physics, Durham University, VIPER RF, Durham University's Physics MES Workshop, Amnovis, and Launch 4 Change. The success of the two-stage configuration and sustainer recovery is a major milestone for DUSF’s solid rocketry program, and we look forward to seeing where the experience gained from this launch will take us next year.

Is English an Ethnicity?

Over the past decade, the issue of immigration has consumed vast swathes of media attention and parliamentary debate time. Often this ink and air time is spent debating the minute details of individual proposals, leaving more fundamental things underdiscussed. For instance, what does it mean to be English?

Some people are very clear. To be English is to belong to the ethnicity for whom England is home. Reform UK MP for Fareham and Waterlooville Suella Braverman embodied this attitude when she said that she can't be English because her family is not from England. This is despite her being born in Harrow. Under this view, Englishness cannot be revoked, renounced, or acquired, and is quite separate from citizenship.

There are a few alternatives to this ethnic conception of the nation. One is that English people belong to an English culture. English people watch royal weddings, celebrate St George's Day in primary school, and know their parish's vicar. Alternatively, Englishness is about land: if this green and pleasant land is your home, then you're English. Either way, one can become and unbecome English if one wishes.

Often in discussions about immigration an essential disagreement is about who belongs here, and who is capable of belonging here. Can someone become English by adopting some aspect of culture, or is Englishness only transmitted by blood from parent to child?

We are proud to announce the successful launch of our Atmos payload as part of the 2026 Launch 4 Change competition! Atmos used digital holography to study airborne particles in real time, with air drawn in and passed through a high-power laser. The scattered light was captured to reconstruct detailed images of each particle, letting us build a detailed picture of the particulate makeup of our air. 

We are also proud to continue being part of Launch 4 Change - an outreach initiative giving students across the UK opportunities to engage with both rocket and climate science! Over this year there have been 10 university designed & launched experimental climate payloads, and 47 schools and youth groups mentored by the universities through their participation in the UK Youth Rocketry Challenge (UKROC).

It was fantastic to see the collaboration and shared enthusiasm between all the university teams at the Launch 4 Change 26 event! A huge thank you to all those involved in the development and support of our participation in the competition this year!
